Jake gestured broadly at the hallway around them, water sloshing at his calves. "This is insulting, honestly. She's not even—" "Jake." "—being creative about it, She's just—" Orela whipped around. “Can you fucking not?” Jake blinked. “What?” “I swear to every crawling god in this place, if you piss Her off more...” A crack split the wall to his left. Not fast. Not dramatic. Just a long slow fracture opening across the plaster from ceiling to baseboard, a deliberate and unhurried thing, trailing a thin seep of dark water from its edges like a signature. It bled down the wall and joined the water at their feet without ceremony. The hallway went very quiet, the crack pulsing once then settling. David turned away from the crack, his breath settling awkward and sharp in his chest. “Don’t think She appreciates you shit-talking Her.” Orela’s mouth was a tight line. “Maybe don’t provoke the possessed demon school until after we find a way out of it?” Jake gave a noncommittal grunt and turned back to the hall ahead, the flashlight finally landing on the warped shape of the front exit. The front door looked like it had been underwater for years. The wood had swollen into something barely recognizable — bloated and dark, the grain split in long weeping lines, the hinges reduced to rust suggestions that had long since fused to the frame. Mold trailing up the frame like veins. Metal and wood warped, paint bubbling in patches where water had soaked up from the base. Handles gleamed slickly. It looked less like a door now and more like something exhumed from the bottom of a lake. Leon ran his hand along the edge of the frame, checking the gap — or rather, checking for where the gap should logically have been. The seal was complete. "Still swollen shut. Could maybe force it, but..." He shook his head. "She’s got it tight." They crashed against it together, shoulders bruising, knuckles white around the warped handles. The frame groaned but didn’t give. The impact landed with that same swallowed quality that everything in this building had, sound dying before it could properly echo, the force going somewhere that wasn't even remotely useful. David bounced off the wood, water splashing against him as he staggered back, and something in his chest pulled wrong. He came away coughing — a hard, wet sound that had been building since the pipe hallway and had finally found its moment. "You alright?" Orela asked. "Fine," David rasped, waving her off as he fought back another wave. He rolled his shoulder, grit in his voice. "Just need a better angle." The next crash echoed flatly through the hall, but the doors didn’t move. Only the building seemed to groan louder, the heavily frosted glass of the windows flexing visibly in their frames. They tried again, straining, shoving, water slapping against their thighs with every surge, but the entryway held. Swollen. Bound. Denied. Nothing. Again. Still nothing. The hinges groaned in complaint. The crowbar idea was, theoretically, a good one. In practice, the door presented a significant obstacle to the theory — specifically, the complete absence of any gap to wedge the crowbar into. The seal was total, wood swollen flush against frame, and getting any kind of purchase meant chipping at the surface first. Wood flaked off in damp curls, but the door refused to budge. Leon jammed the tool into the edge, grunting with effort as he tried to lever the door free. David threw his weight in behind him, but the frame was a solid mass. No gap. No give. Leon braced with the crowbar again, gritting his teeth as he levered the swollen seam. David slammed his shoulder over and over, water splashing high with each hit. Orela tried to keep the light steady, her beam jerking with every shudder. The water had found their knees. David slammed his shoulder into the door again and had to pause against it, coughing, low and harsh, hand to his chest. Spitting out a mouthful of dark water, he resumed efforts again, trying to focus. Orela hovered nearby, eyes darting between the wall leak and David’s poorly masked pause. “This isn’t working. It’s not going to open,” she said softly. “We need to try the back exit.” His hands tightened on the crowbar. They had been at this door for — he didn't know how long. Long enough that his shoulder had moved from insistent to genuinely angry. Long enough that the small pile of waterlogged wood chips floating away from their feet represented real effort, real time, and he was not interested in walking away from it. "Just a little more," he said. "We're close." Dwight’s gaze darted down. The water was higher, having crept past his knees when he wasn’t paying attention. His breath hitched. He shook his head, words tumbling out too fast. "We’re wasting time. We have to move, try another exit. If we stay here..." He reached toward Orela’s flashlight, tugging at her sleeve as if to pull the beam with him. Panic edged his voice. "We have to go. Now." Leon braced harder against the lever, jaw set. "It’s just wood. It’ll give. I’ve broken worse. We stop now, it’ll open the second we walk away." His voice was calm, but iron. He wasn’t quitting. Not yet. “You guys are going to hurt yourselves like that! We need to try the other door!” David slammed his shoulder in again, wincing at the vibration through bone. "He’s right, we can’t stop.
